title: Amos 5:18–27
context: The LORD pronounces woe on those who long for the day of the LORD, expecting it to be bright for them. It will be darkness, not light. He rejects feasts, offerings, and songs, and calls for justice to roll on like rivers. The section ends with a question about the wilderness years and a sentence of exile “beyond Damascus”. Stephen’s speech in Acts 7:42–43 cites verses 25–27 in a form that differs in wording, including “beyond Babylon”; readers can note the difference without forcing a harmonization. Shared ground: empty worship and the day of the LORD are common concerns of both traditions here, with no tradition fork.

verses.text: “Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD! Why do you long for the day of the LORD? It is darkness, and not light.
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD!” Arminian readers see presumption exposed: the people assumed the day would vindicate them, but their own unfaithfulness put them on the wrong side of it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same reversal and stress that God’s judgment begins with those who claim his name. Shared ground: the day of the LORD is “darkness, and not light” for the unrepentant, and covenant privilege does not guarantee safety.

verses.text: As if a man fled from a lion, and a bear met him; or he went into the house and leaned his hand on the wall, and a snake bit him.
verses.arminianNotes: A man flees a lion, meets a bear, then is bitten by a snake in his own house. Arminian readers see a vivid picture of inescapable judgment for those who refuse to turn, with no refuge left when the day comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same certainty of judgment and the futility of escape. Shared ground: the parable warns that what feels like safety, even one’s own house, gives no protection on that day.

verses.text: Won’t the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light? Even very dark, and no brightness in it?
verses.arminianNotes: “Won’t the day of the LORD be darkness, and not light?” The question repeats verse 18 for emphasis. Arminian readers see the repetition pressing the warning home while there is still time to hear it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also hear repetition as emphasis and note that the day is “very dark, and no brightness in it” for those under judgment. Shared ground: hope in the day of the LORD must rest on a right relationship with the LORD, not on national identity.

verses.text: I hate, I despise your feasts, and I can’t stand your solemn assemblies.
verses.arminianNotes: “I hate, I despise your feasts”. Arminian readers hear God rejecting worship cut off from justice; the feasts themselves were commanded, but performed by oppressors they become hateful to him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear the same rejection of hypocritical worship and stress that God looks on the heart and life of the worshiper. Shared ground: this is a common warning about empty worship, and both traditions apply it to the church today.

verses.text: Yes, though you offer me your burnt offerings and meal offerings, I will not accept them; neither will I regard the peace offerings of your fat animals.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD will not accept burnt offerings, meal offerings, or peace offerings. Arminian readers see that sacrifice without obedience cannot please God, echoing other prophetic warnings that he desires faithfulness more than ritual.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see offerings as signs that lose their meaning when severed from faith and righteousness. Shared ground: God does not reject sacrifice in principle; he rejects sacrifice offered by people who trample the poor.

verses.text: Take away from me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps.
verses.arminianNotes: “Take away from me the noise of your songs!” Arminian readers note the stark word noise: music meant as praise becomes a disturbance to God when the singers’ lives contradict their words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same contradiction and apply it to all worship that honors God with lips while hearts are far away. Shared ground: the harps are silenced because the people’s lives do not match their songs.

verses.text: But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
verses.arminianNotes: “But let justice roll on like rivers, and righteousness like a mighty stream.” Arminian readers see God’s desire for justice that never dries up, a life of righteousness that grace makes possible in his people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see justice and righteousness as the fruit God requires and produces in those who truly know him. Shared ground: this verse is one of the clearest statements in the prophets that worship and justice belong together.

verses.text: “Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: “Did you bring to me sacrifices and offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel?” Interpreters debate whether the question expects no, yes, or a qualified answer. Arminian readers leave it open while hearing the point that sacrifice was never the heart of the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the debate and see the question pointing to the wilderness relationship of trust rather than ritual alone. Shared ground: the question exposes Israel’s history of divided loyalty and prepares for the charge in verse 26.

verses.text: You also carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel “carried the tent of your king and the shrine of your images, the star of your god”. The exact names and objects behind this verse are debated, and Acts 7:43 renders it differently. Arminian readers keep the main point: idolatry made by their own hands.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the details loosely and stress that the people worshiped gods “which you made for yourselves.” Shared ground: idolatry, not only hypocrisy, stands behind the LORD’s rejection of their worship.

verses.text: Therefore I will cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus,” says the LORD, whose name is the God of Armies.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I will cause you to go into captivity beyond Damascus,” says the LORD. Arminian readers see exile as the consequence of persistent idolatry and injustice. Acts 7:43 says “beyond Babylon”; the difference can be noted without merging the two.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sentence as certain, sealed by “whose name is the God of Armies.” Shared ground: the God who rules all armies can send his people far beyond their borders, and his judgment reaches beyond the next kingdom to the north.
